subject: physical-education
unitTitle: Stress Management, Mental Skills, and Movement
essentialQuestion: What does movement do for a difficult week, and what does it not do?

prompts.prompt: Explain the critical features or key principle of movement as a regulation tool and its realistic limits in your own words.
Demonstrate or fully describe attention, arousal, and performance under pressure using a version your body and setting allow. A described or adapted version earns full credit.
Apply routines, breathing, and refocusing techniques in a new situation and explain the decision or adjustment you made.
Analyze a plausible technique fault, tactical error, or unsafe choice involving motivation, discipline, and what to do when both are gone; correct it and explain why.
Connect the difference between healthy commitment and compulsive activity with when a difficulty needs support beyond movement and explain how one affects the other.

Present the strongest evidence from the unit task: Build a movement-and-regulation toolkit with a routine for a good week, a routine for a hard week, and a written statement of when the learner would seek support beyond movement.
Identify one thing you can now do or direct yourself, one adjustment that improved it, and one next goal you set for yourself.

adaptationChoices: Every technique has a seated, still, low-intensity, and silent version; the learner selects what their body and setting allow.
accommodationNote: Access supports may change format, pacing, intensity, range, equipment, setting, or response mode without changing the standard being assessed. An adapted or described performance is full credit, not partial credit.
neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
